title: RPA vs agentic automation: which does your ops workflow need?
description: Which ops workflows need RPA bots, AI agents, both or neither: dated prices, reliability studies, who approves exceptions.
topic: RPA vs agentic automation for operations
job: decide whether a workflow needs RPA bots, AI agents, or both
verdict: Use RPA if the steps are fixed, high-volume and run on stable screens, especially old apps with no API[^46][^26].
Use an agent if the work means reading messy documents or making judgment calls, and a person checks the result[^27][^17].
Use both if documents feed a system: the agent reads and decides, the bot executes, people approve exceptions[^17][^6].
Use neither if the app has an API, the process keeps changing, or volume is too low to pay back[^46][^42].
Either way, people approve payments and exceptions; an agent can't be held responsible for a mistake[^38][^27].

summary: An RPA bot repeats a fixed script exactly, while an AI agent picks its next step from the input, so its path can vary[^16][^43]. Agents handle messy documents and judgment calls; bots are steadier on stable screens with fixed steps[^27][^46][^42].

tables.title: How do RPA bots and AI agents differ in practice?
tables.intro: RPA means robotic process automation: software robots that work an app's screen the way a person does[^46]. An API is a direct data link between systems, with no screen involved[^46]. Gartner's one-line split: agents where decisions are needed, automation for routine workflows[^26].

rows.name: How it works
cells: Follows a fixed script of clicks and keystrokes, through any app's screen[^46][^43]
Reads the input, then picks its next step from its instructions, tools and context[^43][^16]

rows.name: Same input twice
cells: Same output every time. Microsoft's words for its fixed flows[^16]
The path can differ. In 2024 tests, agents finished the same retail task in all 8 tries under 25% of the time[^30]

rows.name: Best at
cells: Stable, high-volume rule steps, including old apps with no API (Zapier's view)[^46][^26]
Messy documents and judgment calls where several answers are acceptable and errors get caught[^27][^17]

rows.name: How it breaks
cells: A changed screen or field stops it. UiPath itself names changing interfaces as the challenge[^5][^42]
Invents values for fields that should stay empty and loses track in long tasks[^9]

rows.name: How you pay
cells: Mostly a flat fee per bot, such as $150 a month, read 26 Nov 2026[^10]
Metered per model call, credit or run, so volume sets the bill[^2][^13][^22]

rows.name: Main control
cells: The person who builds a bot doesn't move it to production. Keep a log for each unattended bot[^40][^41]
Access to only what the task needs, and a person approves high-impact actions such as payments[^37][^38]

tables.title: What do published studies say about reliability?
tables.intro: Bot figures come from vendor-paid surveys from 2019 and 2020. No neutral, recent survey of bot breakage turned up, so treat them as dated[^28][^29]. Agent scores rose fast, but consistency on repeat runs is the thing to test[^30][^31].

rows.name: Survey paid for by Pega, an RPA vendor, 2019
cells: 509 firms using RPA[^28]
87% of RPA users had bot failures; 41% said maintaining bots took more time than expected[^28]. Vendor-paid and dated

rows.name: Survey paid for by Tricentis, a testing vendor, 2020
cells: Firms using RPA[^29]
45% of surveyed firms dealt with bot breakage weekly or more often[^29]. Vendor-paid and dated

rows.name: Welsh Government automation discovery report
cells: Public-sector teams[^42]
Bots broke when screens changed; frequent fixes can wipe out the return on unstable processes[^42]

rows.name: τ-bench, ICLR 2025 (academic)

GPT-4o agents solved under 50%; under 25% succeeded on all 8 repeat tries in retail[^30]

Agents 67-85% on simple tasks vs 97.9% for people; 9-19% on complex workflows vs 61.2%[^9]. Vendor-authored

recipes.name: 1. Small AP (accounts payable) or ops team on Microsoft 365: invoices into an old system (both)
recipes.when: A team keying PDF invoices into a finance system (ERP) with no API. From 1 Nov 2026, new Microsoft licences carry no seeded AI Builder credits, so page reading draws Copilot Credits[^15][^13].
flow: Ops lead: time today's keying and count errors for two weeks, as the baseline to beat
AP clerk: save incoming invoices to one shared folder
AI document step: pull vendor, PO (purchase order) number and amounts from each page[^13]
Unattended desktop bot: key matched invoices into the finance system[^10]
Controller: approve every mismatch in a built-in approval step before it posts[^16][^38]
Ops lead: check the run log and the mismatch rate each week[^40]
Ops lead: run it on one team's invoices for a month before adding others
recipes.cost: A bot is $150 a month paid yearly, or $3.00 per unattended run, read 26 Nov 2026[^10][^11]. Reading a page costs 8 credits, about $0.08, so 1,300 pages a month is about $104 (our arithmetic)[^13][^14].

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size, document-heavy intake: claims, orders or onboarding (agent reads, bot writes)
recipes.when: Mixed documents arrive in many formats and someone has to judge what each one is. All three platforms document this agent-plus-robot pattern[^6][^17][^25].
flow: Agent: sort each document and pull the fields the case needs[^6][^25]
Bot: write the checked fields into your main system, such as the claims, order or HR system[^6]
Intake or claims lead: approve every case above a set amount, as a fixed human step[^8]
Named reviewer: clear the agent's unclear cases from an escalation queue[^7]
Ops lead: review error and escalation rates monthly, and whether each step still pays[^40]
recipes.cost: UiPath bills 0.2 Platform Units per standard model call; its only public unit price is £900 per 1,000, UK public-sector list[^2][^4]. Automation Anywhere charges 20 AI Credits per agent run, read 26 Nov 2026[^22].

recipes.name: 3. Stable, high-volume reconciliation or data moves (bot or API only)
recipes.when: The task has one right answer and the screens rarely change. Gartner says agents are far less suited where only one correct answer exists[^27][^16].
flow: Controller: write the matching rules and the tolerance for each account
Analyst: build an API flow where one exists, or an unattended bot where it doesn't[^46][^10]
Bot: match items and send breaks to an exceptions queue
Accountant: clear every break and note the reason
Controller: sign off the reconciliation; a second person moves bot changes to production[^40]
recipes.cost: A Power Automate bot is $150 a month, paid yearly, read 26 Nov 2026[^10]. Each bot runs one flow at a time, so parallel runs need more bots[^10].

humanRole: Controller or AP lead: approves every payment an agent drafts. Microsoft's own guidance has AI draft the payment and a manager approve it[^38][^37].
Ops lead: owns the exception queue. Unclear cases go to a named person or group, never to whoever is free by default[^7][^8].

Bot builder and approver are different people: one builds or changes a bot, another moves it to production[^40][^41]. Keep a bot inventory; Microsoft's audit log records flow changes, not each run[^18].
One named owner per automation: agents can't be held responsible, and a tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's answer[^27][^35].

example.input: Illustrative: an AP clerk keys 300 vendor invoices a week from PDFs into an in-house finance system (ERP) with no API. Each one means reading vendor, PO and amounts, then typing them in[^13][^10].
example.output: A document step pulls the fields and a bot keys matched invoices into the system[^13][^10]. An agent suggests coding for invoices with no PO. The controller approves anything unmatched or over a set amount before it posts[^8][^38].

watchOuts: Buying rebranded bots as agents: Gartner calls this agent washing and counts about 130 real agentic vendors among thousands[^26]. Ask for a demo where different inputs take different paths.

Trusting one good demo: agents vary from run to run, and complex screen workflows scored 9-19% in a UiPath researchers' test[^30][^9]. Run 20-50 of your real cases several times and measure consistency.
Putting a bot on an unstable screen: 45% of firms dealt with broken bots weekly or more, in a vendor-paid 2020 survey[^29]. Use an API where one exists, and budget for upkeep[^42][^40].

Giving an agent write access with no gate: one agent reportedly deleted a production database during a code freeze[^36][^34]. Give agents accounts that reach only what the task needs and human approval before money moves or records change[^37][^38].

Not counting metered costs: agents bill per call, credit or run, and Gartner names rising costs as a top reason projects get cancelled[^2][^13][^26]. Log calls per run in the trial and set spend alerts.
Assuming the vendor owns the mistake: a tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's wrong answer[^35]. Name one human owner for each automation before go-live[^27][^39].

faq.a: No: Gartner still says to use automation for routine workflows and agents where decisions are needed[^26]. UiPath, Microsoft and Automation Anywhere all still sell robots, now next to agents[^1][^10][^21].
Not for stable, rule-based steps, because Gartner says agents are far less suited where only one correct answer exists[^27]. Vendors now run bots and agents together in one flow[^6][^17].

faq.q: Can RPA bots and AI agents work together?
faq.a: Yes, and it's the pattern all three big vendors document. Microsoft describes workflows that call agents and agents that use workflows as tools[^17][^6][^25].

faq.q: What is the difference between an AI agent and an RPA bot?
faq.a: An RPA bot runs the same fixed steps every time, while an AI agent decides its next step from the input[^16][^43]. So a bot gives the same output for the same input, but an agent handles messy work and can vary between runs[^16][^30].

faq.q: Where does an agent earn its keep over plain RPA?
faq.a: On messy inputs and judgment steps, with a narrow list of allowed actions[^17][^27].

faq.q: How much does an AI agent cost to run compared with a bot?
faq.a: A bot is a flat fee, about $150 a month on Power Automate[^10]. An agent is metered, about $0.04-$0.05 per action in Copilot Studio by our math[^13][^14]. Agent cost rises with every action, so at pay-as-you-go rates 3,000 actions a month cost the same as one bot[^10][^13][^14].

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a platform when the process is standard and you have no automation team[^44][^45]. Menlo Ventures found 76% of enterprise AI use cases were bought in 2025, up from 53% in 2024[^44]. MIT NANDA found bought tools reached deployment about twice as often, from 52 interviews, correlation only[^45].
buyVsBuild.build: Build your own flows on a platform when your rules and data are the edge and you need control of each step[^16][^3]. All three let you bring your own model, which moves token costs to your model provider[^2][^23]. For old systems, Gartner says redesigning the workflow often beats bolting on agents[^26].

pickElse: The app has an API or a built-in connector: use a cloud flow, not a screen bot[^46][^11]. Zapier says RPA mostly remains for old systems without APIs (a vendor's view)[^46].
The process is broken or keeps changing: fix it first. Gartner advises rethinking the workflow, and unstable processes eat bot returns in upkeep[^26][^42].
Volume is too low to pay back: keep it manual and review it yearly. COSO says to check regularly whether a bot adds measurable value[^40][^42].
One person needs a lookup or a summary: use an AI assistant, not an agent or a bot. Gartner reserves assistants for simple retrieval[^26].

sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Not sure which workflows need a bot, an agent or neither?
offer.body: Give a bot fixed, high-volume steps on stable screens and an agent messy documents or judgment calls; use neither if the app has an API. In a free 30-minute call we sort your manual workflows into bot, agent, both or neither. You leave with the first one to pilot.

reviews.notes: Wants to know which workflow gets a bot, an agent or neither, and how to prove it worked. The bottom line answers in four 'use X if' lines; the three builds name who does each step. No before-and-after measure was in the invoice build, so added 'time today's keying and count errors for two weeks' as the first step. FAQ questions were seen on r/rpa (Sep 2025), r/automation, r/AI_Agents (Feb 2025) and Zapier's own FAQ on this topic.

Reads on a phone. Cut jargon a non-IT reader would stall on: 'least-privilege' became 'access to only what the task needs', 'system of record' became 'your main system', ERP is spelled out as the finance system, and RPA and API are defined in the first table. Every cell is two sentences or fewer.

Asks whether one unit can pilot first and what it costs that unit. Added a one-team, one-month pilot step to the invoice build, and a monthly cost for 1,300 pages (about $104, our arithmetic, labelled). The own-data table shows the break-even between pay-per-run and a flat bot (50 runs a month). No sourced time-saved figure exists, so none is claimed.

Read as the controller or head of AP whose team would run the invoice bot. Wants to know who approves and what the auditor sees. Every build ends in a named sign-off. Added that Microsoft's audit log records flow changes, not each run, so the controller knows run evidence lives elsewhere. Bot surveys are labelled vendor-paid and dated; UI-CUBE is labelled as written by UiPath researchers.

Steve decides in 10 seconds: the title is his question and the bottom line gives four picks plus a fifth line saying people keep payments and exceptions. He distrusts hype; the Gartner cancellation figure is labelled a forecast and agent washing is a watch-out. US prices are dated; where only UK public-sector list prices exist, the page says so. The offer says what he leaves with: workflows sorted and the first one to pilot. No case from a firm his size exists in the research, so the example is marked illustrative.

answers.recipes: Invoice keying into an old system fits both, messy document intake fits an agent that reads and a bot that writes, and stable reconciliation fits a bot or API[^10][^6][^46].
answers.human-role: Your people keep control: the controller approves every payment an agent drafts, the ops lead owns exceptions, builder and approver stay separate, and each automation has one named owner[^38][^7][^40][^27].
answers.example: On 300 invoices a week, a bot keys matched invoices into an old finance system, an agent suggests coding when there's no PO, and the controller approves exceptions[^13][^10][^8].
answers.what-goes-wrong: Teams go wrong by buying rebranded bots as agents, trusting one good demo, putting bots on unstable screens, giving agents ungated write access, and ignoring metered costs[^26][^30][^29][^37][^2].
answers.something-else: Pick neither when the app has an API, the process keeps changing, volume is too low to pay back, or one person just needs a lookup or summary[^46][^26][^40].
answers.table-1: An RPA bot follows a fixed script on an app's screen, while an AI agent reads the input and picks its next step, so its path can differ[^46][^43][^16].
answers.table-2: Bots mostly cost a flat fee, such as Microsoft's $150 a month, while agents are metered per model call, credit or run[^10][^2][^13][^22].
answers.table-3: Bots break when screens change, and agents still vary between runs, finishing complex screen workflows only 9-19% of the time in one vendor-authored test[^29][^42][^30][^9].
answers.own-data: One Microsoft bot is $150 a month, one unattended run is $3.00, and one agent action is about $0.04-$0.05 by our math[^10][^11][^13][^14].
